name: Tibial plateau fracture
summary: An intra-articular fracture of the proximal tibia caused by axial load combined with valgus or varus, from a low-energy fall in older adults or high-energy trauma. Compartment syndrome and soft tissue injury are common.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 10 per 100,000 per year; peaks at 40–60 years

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Ottawa knee rules to trigger radiographs (Sn 0.99)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs then CT for fracture planning; MRI shows soft tissue injury

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Protected weight-bearing 6–12 weeks; return to sport ~7 months or longer

overview:
Tibial plateau fractures are intra-articular fractures of the weight-bearing surface of the proximal tibia. They have a bimodal pattern: high-energy injuries in younger men and low-energy falls in older women with osteoporotic bone, with an overall incidence of about 10 per 100,000 per year [r1]. The fracture pattern, described by the Schatzker classification, reflects the direction of force: axial load with valgus produces lateral plateau split and depression fractures, while varus and high-energy axial loads produce medial and bicondylar fractures [r2].

These are not simply bone injuries. On MRI, almost every operatively treated plateau fracture has associated soft tissue injury, most often to the lateral meniscus, the cruciate and collateral ligaments and the posterolateral corner [r3]. Acute compartment syndrome complicates about 3% overall and is more frequent in bicondylar (Schatzker VI) fractures [r4]. Physiotherapists see these patients after fixation or during non-operative management, where the priorities are early range of motion, protected and progressive weight-bearing, quadriceps recovery and recognition of complications [r8].

epidemiology.text: In a population-based Danish study, the incidence of tibial plateau fractures was 10.3 per 100,000 per year, the mean age was 52.6 years, and the most common pattern was the lateral split-depression (AO 41-B3, 35%). Men under 50 had a higher incidence than women, but incidence rose sharply in women over 50, consistent with osteoporotic fractures from low-energy falls [r1]. In an MRI study of operatively treated fractures, the lateral split-depression (Schatzker II) was the most common pattern (60%) [r3]. Plateau fractures also accompany a quarter of multiligament knee injuries in major trauma [r12].

intrinsic: Female sex and age over 50 (osteoporosis; potentially modifiable through bone health) [r1]
Low bone mineral density and falls risk (modifiable)
extrinsic: Falls from standing height or from height
Pedestrian struck by a vehicle bumper at knee height

mechanism.summary: Most plateau fractures result from an axial load through the extended or slightly flexed knee combined with a valgus (or, less often, varus) force. The femoral condyle acts like a hammer on the plateau below it: valgus drives the lateral femoral condyle into the lateral plateau, splitting the cortex and depressing the articular surface. In dense young bone the plateau tends to split; in osteoporotic bone it tends to depress. Varus loading produces medial plateau fractures, which are often higher energy and may be fracture-dislocations; pure high-energy axial loads produce bicondylar fractures [r2].
sequence: The person lands on, or is struck on, the leg with the knee extended or slightly flexed and the foot fixed.
Body weight (or impact energy) is transmitted axially down the femur.
A valgus force (e.g. a bumper striking the lateral knee, or landing with the knee collapsing inward) concentrates load on the lateral compartment.
The lateral femoral condyle impacts the lateral tibial plateau, which is weaker than the medial side.
The cortex splits (Schatzker I) and/or the articular surface is driven down into the soft metaphyseal bone (II–III).
The lateral meniscus may be torn or trapped in the fracture, and the MCL is stretched on the tension (medial) side [r3].
A lipohaemarthrosis forms as marrow fat and blood leak into the joint; the person cannot weight-bear.

variants.name: Low-energy fall in older adults
variants.description: A fall from standing height with a valgus twist in osteoporotic bone, typically producing depression or split-depression fractures [r1].

variants.name: Bumper (fender) injury
variants.description: A car bumper strikes the lateral knee of a standing pedestrian, driving it into valgus with axial load.

variants.name: High-energy axial load
variants.description: Falls from height or vehicle crashes producing bicondylar fractures (Schatzker V–VI) with high compartment syndrome risk [r4].

variants.name: Varus / fracture-dislocation
variants.description: Medial plateau fractures (Schatzker IV) from varus load behave like knee dislocations and carry neurovascular risk [r12].

anatomy.text: The tibial plateau consists of the medial and lateral condyles separated by the intercondylar eminence (tibial spines), where the cruciates attach. The medial plateau is larger, concave and stronger; the lateral plateau is smaller, convex and higher, and more often fractures. Each plateau is covered by hyaline cartilage and a meniscus, which together share load. Beneath the thin subchondral plate lies cancellous metaphyseal bone that compacts easily under load, which is why depressed fragments stay depressed and need elevation and bone graft or substitute. The anterior and lateral compartments of the leg lie just below the plateau and the common peroneal nerve winds around the fibular neck [r2,r4].

structures.name: Lateral tibial plateau
structures.role: Convex weight-bearing surface of the lateral compartment; the most commonly fractured part [r3]

structures.name: Medial tibial plateau
structures.role: Larger, stronger surface carrying most load; fractures here imply higher energy [r2]

structures.name: Articular cartilage
structures.role: Distributes load; injured at impact and the main driver of post-traumatic osteoarthritis

structures.name: Menisci
structures.role: Share and spread load; the lateral meniscus is often torn or trapped in the fracture [r3]

structures.name: Collateral and cruciate ligaments
structures.role: Stability; injured in most operative fractures [r3]

structures.name: Leg compartments and common peroneal nerve
structures.role: At risk from swelling (compartment syndrome) and stretch in high-energy fractures [r4]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
The plateau fails when compressive and shear loads exceed the strength of the subchondral plate and cancellous bone. Cortical splitting and articular depression disrupt joint congruity; a step or gap in the cartilage surface and malalignment both concentrate load and accelerate degeneration. The impact also kills chondrocytes and damages cartilage matrix beyond the visible fracture. Fracture healing in this metaphyseal bone is generally reliable when fragments are reduced and stabilised, but depressed fragments can subside if loaded too early, and articular damage remains [r2,r10].

Soft tissue injury is the rule rather than the exception. In 103 operatively treated fractures, only 1% had no soft tissue injury on MRI; 77% had a complete tear or avulsion of at least one cruciate or collateral ligament, 91% had lateral meniscus pathology, 44% medial meniscus tears and 68% posterolateral corner injury [r3]. Bleeding and swelling within the tight leg compartments can raise pressure enough to cause acute compartment syndrome, which occurred in 3.1% of 1119 fractures and was associated with younger age and Schatzker VI fractures [r4].

structures.name: Tibial plateau (bone)
structures.effect: Split, depression or both; bicondylar fractures may separate the metaphysis from the diaphysis [r2]

structures.name: Articular cartilage
structures.effect: Impact injury, steps and gaps; long-term risk of osteoarthritis and arthroplasty [r10]

structures.name: Lateral meniscus
structures.effect: Torn, detached or incarcerated in the fracture in most operative cases [r3]

structures.name: Ligaments and posterolateral corner
structures.effect: Cruciate or collateral tear/avulsion in 77% and PLC injury in 68% of operative fractures [r3]

structures.name: Leg compartments
structures.effect: Acute compartment syndrome in about 3%, more often with Schatzker VI fractures [r4]

muscles.name: Quadriceps
muscles.effect: Marked arthrogenic muscle inhibition and atrophy from haemarthrosis, pain, surgery and weeks of protected weight-bearing [r11].

muscles.name: Calf and hip muscles
muscles.effect: Disuse atrophy during non-weight-bearing; calf weakness contributes to gait deficits.

muscles.name: Anterior and lateral compartment muscles
muscles.effect: Ischaemic injury if compartment syndrome develops; necrosis and contracture if decompression is delayed [r4].

cellular.description: Fracture haematoma forms; platelets and inflammatory cells release cytokines and growth factors that recruit mesenchymal cells. Marrow fat and blood fill the joint (lipohaemarthrosis).

Mesenchymal cells differentiate into chondroblasts and osteoblasts. In well-fixed cancellous metaphyseal bone, healing is largely direct, with little visible external callus; the depressed area may be supported by graft or substitute.
Woven bone is replaced by lamellar bone along lines of stress. Damaged articular cartilage does not regenerate and is replaced at best by fibrocartilage.

systems.effect: Compartment syndrome, popliteal artery injury in fracture-dislocations, and venous thromboembolism during immobilisation [r4,r12].
Pain, quadriceps inhibition [r11] and, in high-energy fractures, common peroneal nerve injury.
Weeks of protected weight-bearing cause generalised lower-limb deconditioning, reduced balance and altered gait.
In older adults, the fracture is often a fragility fracture and should prompt osteoporosis assessment [r1].
Fear of falling, prolonged time off work and uncertainty about return to sport affect recovery [r9].

grades.description: Lateral plateau split without depression; typically younger patients with dense bone [r2].
grades.prognosis: Good if undisplaced (non-operative) or well fixed

grades.description: Lateral split with depression of the articular surface; the most common type [r3].
grades.prognosis: Usually ORIF with elevation and grafting; meniscal injury common [r3]

grades.description: Pure central depression of the lateral plateau, typically in osteoporotic bone; MRI suggests pure depression without any cortical split is rare [r3].
grades.prognosis: Elevation and support; risk of subsidence

grades.description: Medial plateau fracture, often higher energy; may be a fracture-dislocation with ligament and neurovascular injury [r12].
Bicondylar fracture with the metaphysis and diaphysis still in continuity.
Bicondylar fracture with metaphyseal–diaphyseal dissociation; highest energy.
grades.prognosis: Strongest predictor of compartment syndrome [r4]; higher arthroplasty risk for bicondylar fractures [r10]

timeframes.summary: Bony union usually takes 3–4 months, but protected loading, cartilage injury and soft tissue damage mean full recovery often takes 6–12 months, and many people do not return to their previous level of sport [r9].

healing.description: Fracture haematoma, swelling, compartment risk highest
Protected weight-bearing while bone unites; early range of motion
Bone remodels; strength and function recover; cartilage changes persist

milestones.label: Knee flexion ≥ 90°
milestones.note: Early range of motion is encouraged after fixation [r8]

milestones.label: Progressive weight-bearing begins (typical)
milestones.note: Earlier in selected cases per surgeon [r7]

milestones.label: Return to demanding sport (typical upper range)

timeframes.returnToSport: About 70% of patients return to sport, with lower rates after open reduction and internal fixation (60%) and frame fixation (52%) than after arthroscopically assisted fixation (83%); the only reported median return time was 6.9 months after ORIF [r9]. Return is guided by union, strength and function rather than time.

symptoms: Immediate knee pain and inability to weight-bear after a fall, a jump or a blow to the side of the knee
Rapid swelling of the knee and upper shin
Pain on any attempt to move the knee
In high-energy injuries: severe leg pain, numbness or tingling in the foot
signs: Bony tenderness over the proximal tibia and joint line
Valgus or varus deformity or instability
Inability to bear weight for four steps
Bruising, abrasions or fracture blisters over the proximal leg

subjective: Mechanism and energy: fall from standing height, fall from height, pedestrian versus car, sport
Ability to weight-bear immediately and since
Leg pain out of proportion, numbness, tingling, or a cold foot
Osteoporosis risk factors and previous fragility fractures
After fixation: surgeon's weight-bearing and range-of-motion instructions, wound status, VTE prophylaxis
observation: Swelling, bruising, fracture blisters and skin integrity
After fixation: wound healing and gait with aids
palpation: Proximal tibia, joint lines and fibular head
rangeOfMotion: After fixation: measure flexion and extension at each session; aim for ≥ 90° flexion by about 4 weeks
strength: Hip and ankle strength during protected weight-bearing
Later: quadriceps and hamstring limb symmetry
neuro: Common peroneal nerve function (dorsiflexion, eversion, dorsal foot sensation) in high-energy fractures
functional: Gait with aids within weight-bearing limits
Later: single-leg squat, hop tests if returning to sport

specialTests.name: Ottawa knee rules
specialTests.purpose: Decide who needs radiographs after acute knee injury
specialTests.procedure: Radiograph if any one is present: age ≥ 55; isolated patellar tenderness; fibular head tenderness; inability to flex to 90°; inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately and in the emergency department.
specialTests.positive: Any criterion present: obtain radiographs. In a validation study the rule was 100% sensitive for 63 clinically important fractures [r6]; a meta-analysis found pooled sensitivity 0.99 and specificity 0.49 [r5].

specialTests.name: Compartment assessment (clinical)
specialTests.procedure: Assess pain severity and progression, compartment firmness, and pain on passive stretch of the toes and ankle; repeat regularly in the first 48–72 hours.
specialTests.positive: Escalating pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment; late signs include sensory loss and weakness. Urgent surgical review.

specialTests.name: Ligament stability examination (once safe)
specialTests.procedure: Varus and valgus stress at 0° and 30°, Lachman and posterior drawer, usually under anaesthesia or after fixation.
specialTests.positive: Laxity indicating collateral, cruciate or posterolateral corner injury, which are common [r3].

clinicalRules.name: Ottawa knee rules
clinicalRules.description: Radiograph if age ≥ 55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90°, or inability to bear weight for four steps [r5,r6].

outcomeMeasures.name: KOOS
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain, symptoms, function, sport and quality of life after fracture

outcomeMeasures.name: Lysholm score
outcomeMeasures.use: Knee function; widely reported after plateau fixation

outcomeMeasures.name: Range of motion and quadriceps strength

imaging.indication: Ottawa rules positive or clinical suspicion
imaging.findings: Split and depression fractures, lipohaemarthrosis (fat–fluid level on a cross-table lateral), alignment
Fragment number, depression depth and posterior involvement for surgical planning

imaging.indication: Suspected occult fracture or significant soft tissue injury
imaging.findings: Meniscal tears and incarceration, ligament and posterolateral corner injuries, which occur in nearly all operative fractures [r3]

imaging.indication: Medial (Schatzker IV) or bicondylar fractures with abnormal pulses or fracture-dislocation

differentials.name: ACL rupture
differentials.distinguishing: Non-contact pivot with rapid haemarthrosis but able to bear some weight; no bony tenderness. A Segond fracture is an avulsion, not a plateau fracture.

differentials.name: Knee dislocation (multiligament injury)
differentials.distinguishing: Multiplanar laxity and neurovascular risk; medial plateau fracture-dislocations overlap with this injury.

differentials.name: MCL sprain
differentials.distinguishing: Valgus mechanism with medial ligament tenderness, can usually bear weight, and Ottawa rules are negative.

differentials.name: Patella fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness and swelling over the patella, extensor lag; tibial plateau non-tender.

differentials.name: Tibial and fibular shaft fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Deformity and tenderness in the shaft rather than at the joint.

differentials.name: Articular cartilage or osteochondral injury
differentials.distinguishing: Haemarthrosis after a twist or impact with focal cartilage loss on MRI; no plateau fracture on CT.

redFlags: Severe or escalating leg pain, pain on passive toe stretch and tense compartments, especially with Schatzker VI or high-energy fractures: suspect acute compartment syndrome. Emergency surgical review for fasciotomy [r4].
Absent or weak pulses, cold foot or ABI < 0.90 with a medial or bicondylar fracture: suspect popliteal artery injury. Emergency vascular assessment [r12].
Foot drop or numbness on the dorsum of the foot: common peroneal nerve injury; document and refer urgently.
Open wound over the fracture: open fracture requiring emergency antibiotics and surgery.

After fixation: wound redness, discharge, fever or rising pain (infection); calf swelling or breathlessness (DVT/PE); new deformity or loss of range (loss of reduction). Arrange urgent medical review.

management.principles: Undisplaced, stable fractures are treated non-operatively with early motion and protected weight-bearing. Displaced, depressed or unstable fractures are usually fixed to restore the articular surface, alignment and stability, with timing dictated by the soft tissues (temporary external fixation is common in high-energy fractures) [r2]. Associated meniscal and ligament injuries are frequent and may be addressed at surgery [r3]. After fixation, early range of motion should be encouraged, post-operative immobilisation appears to offer no benefit, and early weight-bearing is increasingly used in selected cases; the surgeon's fixation determines the loading plan [r7,r8]. Older adults also need falls and bone-health assessment [r1].

medical.name: Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF)
medical.description: Elevation of depressed fragments with bone graft or substitute and plate/screw fixation for displaced or unstable fractures; the most common operative treatment [r2,r9].

medical.name: Arthroscopically assisted reduction and internal fixation (ARIF)
medical.description: For selected lateral split/depression fractures; associated with higher return-to-sport rates (83%) than ORIF (60%) in a systematic review of mainly observational studies [r9].

medical.name: Temporary spanning external fixation and staged surgery
medical.description: Used in high-energy fractures with poor soft tissues or compartment syndrome until definitive fixation is safe [r4].

medical.name: Non-operative treatment
medical.description: Hinged brace, early range of motion and protected weight-bearing for undisplaced, stable fractures or patients unfit for surgery [r2].

medical.name: Fasciotomy for compartment syndrome
medical.description: Emergency decompression when compartment syndrome is diagnosed [r4].

medical.name: Osteoporosis assessment and VTE prophylaxis
medical.description: Bone-health investigation and treatment in older adults with low-energy fractures [r1], and thromboprophylaxis per protocol during reduced mobility.

physio.name: Early range-of-motion exercise
physio.description: Active and active-assisted knee flexion and extension from the first days after fixation (or as allowed in a brace), aiming for ≥ 90° flexion by about 4 weeks [r8].

physio.name: Protected, progressive weight-bearing
physio.description: Traditionally touch- or partial weight-bearing for 6–12 weeks; early weight-bearing appears safe in selected fixation constructs. Follow the surgeon's instructions [r7,r8].

physio.name: Quadriceps strengthening and proprioceptive training
physio.description: Isometric then progressive quadriceps strengthening and balance training throughout rehabilitation [r8]. NMES may help overcome inhibition early [r11].

physio.name: Prolonged post-operative immobilisation
physio.description: Immobilisation after plate fixation does not appear to benefit patients and increases stiffness risk [r8].

physio.name: Gait retraining with aids and falls prevention
physio.description: Teach safe gait within weight-bearing limits and address falls risk in older adults (expert opinion).

education: This is a break into the knee joint itself, so the bone, cartilage and often the meniscus or ligaments are involved.
Moving the knee early is safe and important, but loading must follow your surgeon's plan so the joint surface does not sink.
Bone usually heals in about 3–4 months, but full recovery of strength and function often takes 6–12 months.
Report increasing leg pain, numbness, a cold foot, wound problems or calf swelling straight away.
Some people develop knee arthritis years later; staying strong and active and keeping a healthy weight help.

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation is criteria- and surgeon-guided. Bone protection determines loading; range of motion starts early because stiffness is common and immobilisation has no proven benefit [r8]. Progress weight-bearing according to the fixation and radiographic healing (earlier weight-bearing is increasingly used in selected cases [r7]), then rebuild quadriceps strength, balance and function. Non-operatively managed undisplaced fractures follow the same stages, usually with a hinged brace.

stages.name: Protect & move
goals: Full extension and flexion ≥ 90° by about 4 weeks
precautions: Weight-bearing as prescribed (often touch or partial)
Monitor compartments early, wound, calf (DVT) and nerve function

exercises.name: Heel slides (active-assisted flexion)
exercises.cues: Slide smoothly; stop at a stretch, not pain

exercises.name: Seated ankle range of motion and calf pumps
Hip strengthening in lying (abduction, bridges within limits)

stages.name: Load & restore gait
precautions: Progress weight-bearing in steps guided by symptoms and radiographs

exercises.name: Weight-shift and mini squats (as weight-bearing allows)

progressionCriteria: Full weight-bearing without pain or limp

stages.name: Strength & function
precautions: Introduce impact only after radiographic union and surgeon clearance

exercises.name: Leg press and squat with load

stages.name: Return to sport & high-level activity
goals: Running, landing and agility if appropriate
Return to sport or demanding work
precautions: Monitor effusion and pain with impact; adjust load

exercises.name: Walk–run progression
exercises.dosage: Every second day, building to 20–30 min

criteria: Full or functional range of motion without effusion
Quadriceps and hamstring strength ≥ 90% of the other side
Hop test battery ≥ 90% symmetry with good landing quality

prognosis: Most fractures unite, but function is often not fully restored. About 70% return to sport overall, with lower rates after ORIF and frame fixation [r9]. Post-traumatic osteoarthritis is a major long-term concern: 10 years after operative fixation, 7.3% had undergone total knee arthroplasty compared with 1.8% of matched controls (hazard ratio 5.29), with higher risk in older patients and bicondylar fractures [r10]. Associated meniscal and ligament injuries are common and may contribute to later symptoms [r3]. Compartment syndrome, infection and loss of reduction are the main early complications [r4].
prevention: Falls prevention and osteoporosis assessment and treatment in older adults with low-energy fractures [r1].
Road safety measures for pedestrians and motorcyclists (general advice).
clinicalPearls: An older adult who 'twisted the knee' and cannot weight-bear needs an X-ray: age ≥ 55 alone meets the Ottawa rules [r6].
A fat–fluid level on a cross-table lateral radiograph means an intra-articular fracture until proven otherwise.
Assume a soft tissue injury. Lateral meniscal and ligament injuries accompany almost every operative plateau fracture [r3].
Schatzker VI fractures and younger patients have the highest compartment syndrome risk; listen to pain [r4].
Move early, load as instructed. Stiffness is preventable, subsidence is avoidable [r7,r8].
A medial plateau fracture may be a knee dislocation in disguise. Check pulses and nerves.

animation.title: How a tibial plateau fracture happens

captions.text: An older adult misses the bottom step.
They land heavily on the right leg with the knee almost straight.
Body weight drives straight down the femur as the knee buckles into valgus.
The lateral femoral condyle hammers into the lateral tibial plateau.
Immediate pain, rapid swelling and they cannot stand on the leg.
Zooming into the right knee from the front; lateral is on the left of the screen.
The lateral tibial plateau is smaller and convex, so it fails first under valgus load.
Axial load plus valgus concentrates force on the lateral compartment.
The condyle splits the plateau and drives the joint surface down into soft cancellous bone.
The lateral meniscus is torn or caught in the fracture in most operative cases.
On the opposite side, the MCL is stretched by the valgus force.
Blood and marrow fat leak into the joint: a fat–fluid level on X-ray.
A step in the joint surface concentrates load; restoring it is the aim of fixation.
Healthy cancellous bone: a lattice of trabeculae under a thin subchondral plate.
Compression crushes trabeculae and breaks the subchondral plate.
Bleeding from the marrow forms a fracture haematoma.
Inflammatory cells release signals that recruit bone-forming stem cells.
A soft callus of cartilage and fibrous tissue bridges the fragments.
Callus mineralises into woven bone; by about 3 months the fracture can take full load.
Bone remodels along stress lines, but damaged joint cartilage does not regenerate.
